findings.text: GitHub recommends building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app.
findings.quote: Consider building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app.

findings.text: A user or organization can own a maximum of 100 OAuth apps.
findings.quote: A user or organization can own up to 100 OAuth apps.

findings.text: Navigate to your profile settings.
findings.quote: In the upper-right corner of any page on GitHub, click your profile picture, then click Settings.

findings.text: Click on Developer settings in the sidebar.
findings.quote: In the left sidebar, click Developer settings.

findings.text: Click on OAuth apps.
findings.quote: In the left sidebar, click OAuth apps.

findings.text: Click the button to create a new OAuth app.
findings.quote: Click New OAuth App.

findings.text: Enter the name of your application.
findings.quote: In "Application name", type the name of your app.

findings.text: Enter the homepage URL for your app.
findings.quote: In "Homepage URL", type the full URL to your app's website.

findings.text: Enter the authorization callback URL.
findings.quote: In "Authorization callback URL", type the callback URL of your app.

findings.text: Click the button to register the application.
findings.quote: Click Register application.

findings.text: You can enter a maximum of 10 callback URLs.
findings.quote: You can enter up to 10 callback URLs.

findings.text: Do not use sensitive data such as internal URLs in your OAuth app.
findings.quote: Avoid using sensitive data, such as internal URLs, when creating an OAuth app.

findings.text: The primary rate limit for unauthenticated requests is 60 requests per hour.
findings.quote: The primary rate limit for unauthenticated requests is 60 requests per hour.

findings.text: The primary rate limit for authenticated users is 5,000 requests per hour.
findings.quote: All of these requests count towards your personal rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour.

findings.text: OAuth apps owned or approved by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization have a rate limit of 15,000 requests per hour.
findings.quote: Similarly, requests made on your behalf by a OAuth app that is owned or approved by a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization have a higher rate limit of 15,000 requests per hour if you are a member of the GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization.

findings.text: The rate limit for Git LFS access is 300 requests per minute for unauthenticated requests.
findings.quote: These count towards a separate rate limiting bucket with a limit of 300 requests per minute for unauthenticated requests and 3,000 requests per minute for authenticated requests.

findings.text: The rate limit for Git LFS access is 3,000 requests per minute for authenticated requests.
findings.quote: These count towards a separate rate limiting bucket with a limit of 300 requests per minute for unauthenticated requests and 3,000 requests per minute for authenticated requests.

findings.text: The rate limit for GitHub App installations is 5,000 requests per hour.
findings.quote: GitHub Apps authenticating with an installation access token use the installation's minimum rate limit of 5,000 requests per hour.

findings.text: The rate limit for GitHub App installations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud is 15,000 requests per hour.
findings.quote: If the installation is on a GitHub Enterprise Cloud organization, the installation has a rate limit of 15,000 requests per hour.

findings.text: The rate limit for an OAuth app using its client ID and secret is 5,000 requests per hour.
findings.quote: For these requests, the rate limit is 5,000 requests per hour per OAuth app.

findings.text: The rate limit for GITHUB_TOKEN in GitHub Actions is 1,000 requests per hour per repository.
findings.quote: The rate limit for GITHUB_TOKEN is 1,000 requests per hour per repository.

findings.text: No more than 100 concurrent requests are allowed.
findings.quote: Make too many concurrent requests. No more than 100 concurrent requests are allowed.

findings.text: No more than 900 points per minute are allowed for REST API endpoints.
findings.quote: Make too many requests to a single endpoint per minute. No more than 900 points per minute are allowed for REST API endpoints, and no more than 2,000 points per minute are allowed for the GraphQL API endpoint.

findings.text: No more than 2,000 points per minute are allowed for the GraphQL API endpoint.
findings.quote: Make too many requests to a single endpoint per minute. No more than 900 points per minute are allowed for REST API endpoints, and no more than 2,000 points per minute are allowed for the GraphQL API endpoint.

findings.text: No more than 2,000 OAuth access token requests per hour are allowed for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps.
findings.quote: Make too many OAuth access token requests in a short period of time. No more than 2,000 OAuth access token requests per hour are allowed for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps.

findings.text: Never include your app's client secret in client-side code or in code that runs on a user device.
findings.quote: Never include your app's client secret in client-side code or in code that runs on a user device. The client secret can be used to generate OAuth access tokens for users who have authorized your app, so you should always keep the client secret secure.

findings.text: Access tokens expire after eight hours.
findings.quote: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use.

findings.text: Refresh tokens expire after six months without use.
findings.quote: The access token expires after eight hours, and the refresh token expires after six months without use.

findings.text: The temporary code for the web application flow expires after 10 minutes.
findings.quote: The temporary code will expire after 10 minutes.

findings.text: The device flow user code expires after 15 minutes.
findings.quote: The user must enter a valid code within 15 minutes (or 900 seconds). After 15 minutes, you will need to request a new device authorization code with POST https://github.com/login/device/code.

findings.text: There is a rate limit of 50 device flow submissions per hour per application.
findings.quote: When a user submits the verification code on the browser, there is a rate limit of 50 submissions in an hour per application.

findings.text: There is a limit of ten tokens issued per user/application/scope combination.
findings.quote: There is a limit of ten tokens that are issued per user/application/scope combination, and a rate limit of ten tokens created per hour.

findings.text: There is a rate limit of ten tokens created per hour.
findings.quote: There is a limit of ten tokens that are issued per user/application/scope combination, and a rate limit of ten tokens created per hour.

findings.text: CORS pre-flight requests are not supported.
findings.quote: CORS pre-flight requests (OPTIONS) are not supported at this time.

findings.text: The plain code challenge method is not supported for PKCE.
findings.quote: Must be S256 - the plain code challenge method is not supported.

findings.text: If states do not match during the web flow, the process must be aborted.
findings.quote: If the states don't match, then a third party created the request, and you should abort the process.

findings.text: If a refresh token is invalid or expired, you must send the user through the authorization flow again.
findings.quote: If the refresh token that you specified is invalid or expired, you will receive a bad_refresh_token error. To resolve this error, send the user through the web application flow or device flow again to get a new access token and refresh token.

findings.text: Request a user's GitHub identity via the authorize endpoint.
findings.quote:

findings.text: Exchange the temporary code for an access token.
findings.quote:
Exchange this code for an access token:

POST https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token

findings.text: Use the access token to access the API.
findings.quote:

findings.quote: When you submit your listing for publication, you must read and accept the terms of the GitHub Marketplace Developer Agreement.

findings.text: Listings must include valid contact information for the publisher.
findings.quote: Listings must include valid contact information for the publisher.

findings.text: Listings must have a relevant description of the application.
findings.quote: Listings must have a relevant description of the application.

findings.text: Listings must specify a pricing plan.

findings.text: Listings must have a valid link to a privacy policy.
findings.quote: Listings must have a valid link to a privacy policy.

findings.quote: Listings must provide a method to receive support through a valid support link and/or a support email address.

findings.text: Apps must be publicly available and not in public preview or invite only.
findings.quote: Apps must be publicly available in GitHub Marketplace and cannot be in public preview or available by invite only.

findings.text: Listings must not actively persuade users away from GitHub.
findings.quote: Listings must not actively persuade users away from GitHub.

findings.text: To offer paid plans for your app, the app must be owned by an organization.
findings.quote: To offer paid plans for your app, the app must be owned by an organization and you must have owner permissions in the organization.

findings.text: You must enable two-factor authentication for your organization to get publisher verification.
findings.quote: Ensure that Two-factor authentication is enabled for your organization. For more information, see Requiring two-factor authentication in your organization.

findings.text: You must verify your organization's domain to get publisher verification.
findings.quote: Submit a verified domain and ensure that a "Verified" badge displays on your organization's profile page. For related information, see Verifying or approving a domain for your organization.

findings.text: Navigate to your organization settings.
findings.quote: In the upper-right corner of GitHub, click your profile picture, then click Organizations. Select an organization by clicking it. Under your organization name, click Settings.

findings.text: Access the developer settings for the organization.
findings.quote: At the bottom of the left sidebar, click Developer settings. Under "Developer settings", click Publisher Verification.

findings.text: Submit the verification request.
findings.quote: Click Request Verification. GitHub will review your details and let you know once your publisher verification is complete.

findings.quote: Consider building a GitHub App instead of an OAuth app. GitHub Apps use fine-grained permissions instead of scopes, which give you more control over what your app can do.
